steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on DISYRE, a diffusion-inspired synthetic restoration method for unsupervised anomaly detection in medical images. Cover UAD and its motivation, generative and restoration-based approaches, diffusion models for UAD, synthetic anomaly methods, and end with our contribution.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Unsupervised anomaly detection in medical imaging
- Generative-model approaches and their weaknesses
- Restoration-based methods
- Diffusion models and their use for UAD
- Synthetic anomaly methods
- Contribution: DISYRE

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- UAD in medical imaging
  - detect/localize irregularities without annotations; annotations expensive, challenging
  - prediction: compare test image with learned (often parameterized) healthy distribution
  - anomalies = deviations from healthy distribution
- Generative models
  - variational auto-encoders, generative adversarial networks
  - assumption: can't reconstruct out-of-distribution regions -> reconstruction error marks anomalous pixels
  - often fails: normal data not reconstructed accurately, residual error calibrated as subject-specific bias
  - auto-encoders can reconstruct anomalies too
- Restoration-based
  - Maximum-A-Posteriori (MAP) estimation removes local anomalies
  - followers: two-stage; identify anomalous areas/latents, resample to in-distribution
- Diffusion models
  - state of the art for image generation
  - DDPM: Gaussian noise -> image distribution
  - Langevin dynamics, score function \nabla_{x}\log p(x), iterative denoising
  - score could be pixel-wise anomaly score (where and how to edit to raise likelihood)
  - but trained on Gaussian-noise corruption, doesn't generalize to other anomalies
  - so not favoured for UAD
  - AnoDDPM: simplex noise, multi-scale -> corrects larger anomalous structures
  - DAE authors: coarse noise beats pixel-level noise
  - classifier guidance to restore to expected distribution; needs discriminator with sample-level labels
- Synthetic anomalies
  - Foreign Patch Interpolation (FPI): train segmentation nets on synthetic anomalies in healthy anatomies
  - square region interpolated with patch from another sample, factor \alpha
  - limitation: boundary gradients -> shortcut
  - Poisson Image Interpolation (PII): Poisson image blending on gradients, seamless
  - Naval et al.: soften interpolation factor at boundaries; random shapes for variety
- Contribution
  - DISYRE: Diffusion-Inspired SYnthetic REstoration
  - replace Gaussian noise corruption with synthetic anomaly degradation -> diffusion-like model for UAD and localisation
  - score function generalizes to naturally-occurring medical anomalies; shows how to move test image into healthy distribution
  - noise-free diffusion-like pipelines exist for image generation; first designed for UAD (to our knowledge)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (UAD) in medical image analysis is about detecting and/or localizing irregularities in medical images without needing annotations. This is especially valuable because getting annotations can be expensive and also challenging. In the prediction phase, UAD methods compare a test image with the established distribution, often with a parameterized model of the distribution. If the test image deviates from this healthy distribution, anomalies are detected.

A lot of UAD methods model the expected distribution with generative models like variational auto-encoders or generative adversarial networks. They rely on the assumption that a generative model trained on in-distribution data will not be able to reconstruct out-of-distribution regions, so the reconstruction error can be used to find anomalous pixels. Unfortunately this assumption often fails, because models may not reconstruct normal data accurately and the remaining residual error has to be calibrated as subject-specific bias. Also, auto-encoders are known to be able to reconstruct anomalies as well.

Another option is restoration-based methods, which use Maximum-A-Posteriori (MAP) estimation to remove local anomalies from images. Many approaches followed this idea, often with a two-stage restoration process: first the anomalous areas or latent variables are identified and then they are resampled to be in-distribution.

More recently diffusion models have become the state-of-the-art method for image generation. The most common one is the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM), which builds a mapping from Gaussian noise to a desired image distribution. For this, DDPMs use Langevin dynamics to learn a score function, i.e. \nabla_{x}\log p(x), which can iteratively denoise a sample of Gaussian noise to get a sample from the target image distribution. This kind of score function could be very relevant for UAD, because it can show both where and how to edit the image to increase its likelihood, so it directly acts as a pixel-wise anomaly score. But a standard DDPM learns a score function specific to images corrupted with Gaussian noise, so it does not generalize to correcting images with other types of anomalies.

- Diffusion models for UAD
  - DDPM score not favoured for UAD
  - AnoDDPM: simplex noise, multi-scale -> corrects larger anomalous structures
  - DAE authors: coarse noise beats pixel-level noise
  - classifier guidance to restore to expected distribution; needs discriminator with sample-level labels
- Synthetic anomalies
  - Foreign Patch Interpolation (FPI): train segmentation nets on synthetic anomalies in healthy anatomies
  - square region interpolated with patch from another sample, factor \alpha
  - limitation: boundary gradients -> shortcut
  - Poisson Image Interpolation (PII): Poisson image blending on gradients, seamless
  - Naval et al.: soften interpolation factor at boundaries; random shapes for variety
- Contribution
  - DISYRE: Diffusion-Inspired SYnthetic REstoration
  - replace Gaussian noise corruption with synthetic anomaly degradation -> diffusion-like model for UAD and localisation
  - score function generalizes to naturally-occurring medical anomalies; shows how to move test image into healthy distribution
  - noise-free diffusion-like pipelines exist for image generation; first designed for UAD (to our knowledge)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (UAD) in medical image analysis is about detecting and/or localizing irregularities in medical images without needing annotations. This is especially valuable because getting annotations can be expensive and also challenging. In the prediction phase, UAD methods compare a test image with the established distribution, often with a parameterized model of the distribution. If the test image deviates from this healthy distribution, anomalies are detected.

A lot of UAD methods model the expected distribution with generative models like variational auto-encoders or generative adversarial networks. They rely on the assumption that a generative model trained on in-distribution data will not be able to reconstruct out-of-distribution regions, so the reconstruction error can be used to find anomalous pixels. Unfortunately this assumption often fails, because models may not reconstruct normal data accurately and the remaining residual error has to be calibrated as subject-specific bias. Also, auto-encoders are known to be able to reconstruct anomalies as well.

Another option is restoration-based methods, which use Maximum-A-Posteriori (MAP) estimation to remove local anomalies from images. Many approaches followed this idea, often with a two-stage restoration process: first the anomalous areas or latent variables are identified and then they are resampled to be in-distribution.

More recently diffusion models have become the state-of-the-art method for image generation. The most common one is the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM), which builds a mapping from Gaussian noise to a desired image distribution. For this, DDPMs use Langevin dynamics to learn a score function, i.e. \nabla_{x}\log p(x), which can iteratively denoise a sample of Gaussian noise to get a sample from the target image distribution. This kind of score function could be very relevant for UAD, because it can show both where and how to edit the image to increase its likelihood, so it directly acts as a pixel-wise anomaly score. But a standard DDPM learns a score function specific to images corrupted with Gaussian noise, so it does not generalize to correcting images with other types of anomalies.

For this reason the score function of DDPM has not been favoured when diffusion models are applied to UAD. Instead AnoDDPM replaces Gaussian noise with simplex noise, since simplex noise is multi-scale and this trains the score function to correct larger anomalous structures. This matches what the DAE authors reported, that denoising models trained on reasonably coarse noise did better than ones using pixel-level noise. Another approach uses classifier guidance to push the model to restore the image so it is part of an expected distribution. But this needs a discriminator model trained with sample-level labels.

Apart from generative models, Foreign Patch Interpolation (FPI) proposed training anomaly segmentation networks directly by adding synthetic anomalies to otherwise healthy anatomies. The anomalies are made by interpolating a square region of the sample with a patch taken from a different sample, and the interpolation is controlled with a factor \alpha. One limitation of FPI is that it produces image gradients on the boundaries between the synthetic anomalies and the original images, and the model could use this as a shortcut to identify synthetic anomalies. Poisson Image Interpolation (PII) proposes Poisson image blending to mitigate this, doing the interpolation on the gradients of the image so the anomaly is blended seamlessly with the surrounding area. Naval et al. took a simpler approach and softened the interpolation factor at the boundaries to make the change more gradual, and also generated anomalies with randomly generated shapes to get more variety in the generated anomalies.

Contribution: In this work we introduce DISYRE: Diffusion-Inspired SYnthetic REstoration. We replace the Gaussian noise corruption in diffusion models with a synthetic anomaly degradation process, which allows a diffusion-like model to be used directly for unsupervised anomaly detection and localisation. It learns a score function that generalizes to naturally-occurring medical anomalies and shows how to change a test image to bring it into the healthy distribution. Diffusion-like pipelines without noise have been proposed before for image generation, but to our knowledge this is the first approach designed specifically for UAD.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (UAD) in medical image analysis involves the detection and/or localization of irregularities in medical images without the need for annotations. This approach is particularly valuable since obtaining annotations can be both expensive and challenging [1]. During the prediction phase, UAD methods compare a test image with the established distribution, often using a parameterized model of this distribution. Anomalies are detected when deviations from this healthy distribution are observed in the test image.

Many UAD methods rely on modelling the expected distribution with generative models such as variational auto-encoders [2] or generative adversarial networks [3]. These rely on the assumption that generative models trained on in-distribution data will be unable to reconstruct out-of-distribution regions, so that the reconstruction error can be used to identify anomalous pixels. Unfortunately, this assumption often fails, as models may not accurately reconstruct normal data and the remaining residual error needs to be calibrated as subject-specific bias [2,4]. Furthermore, auto-encoders are known to be able to reconstruct anomalies as well [4].

As an alternative, restoration-based methods [5] use Maximum-A-Posteriori (MAP) estimation to remove local anomalies from images. Many approaches have since followed this idea, often with a two-stage restoration process: first identifying anomalous areas or latent variables and then resampling them to become in-distribution [6,4].

More recently, diffusion models have emerged as the state-of-the-art method for image generation. The most common of these is the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) [7], which constructs a mapping from Gaussian noise to a desired image distribution. To do this, DDPMs leverage Langevin dynamics [7] to learn a score function, i.e. \nabla_{x}\log p(x), which can iteratively denoise a sample of Gaussian noise to produce a sample from the target image distribution. Such a score function is potentially very relevant for UAD, as it can indicate both where and how to edit the image to increase its likelihood, directly acting as a pixel-wise anomaly score. However, since a standard DDPM learns a score function specific to images corrupted with Gaussian noise, it does not generalize to correcting images containing other types of anomalies.

Because of this, DDPM’s score function has not been favoured when applying diffusion models to UAD. AnoDDPM [8] instead replaces Gaussian noise with simplex noise, as the multi-scale nature of simplex noise trains the score function to correct larger anomalous structures. This is consistent with the findings of the DAE [9] authors, who reported that denoising models trained on reasonably coarse noise outperformed those using pixel-level noise. An alternative approach [10] uses classifier guidance to encourage the model to restore the image to be part of an expected distribution. However, this requires training a discriminator model with sample-level labels.

Separately from generative models, Foreign Patch Interpolation (FPI) [11] proposed directly training anomaly segmentation networks by adding synthetic anomalies to otherwise healthy anatomies. The anomalies are generated by interpolating a square region of the sample with a patch extracted from a separate sample, with the interpolation controlled by a factor \alpha. One limitation of FPI is that it produces image gradients on the boundaries between synthetic anomalies and original images, which the model could exploit as a shortcut to identify synthetic anomalies. Poisson Image Interpolation (PII) [12] proposes Poisson image blending to mitigate this, performing the interpolation on the gradients of the image and seamlessly blending the anomaly with the surrounding area. Naval et al. [13] took a simpler approach, softening the interpolation factor at the boundaries to make a more gradual change, and generating anomalies with randomly generated shapes to produce greater variety.

Contribution: In this work we introduce DISYRE: Diffusion-Inspired SYnthetic REstoration. Replacing the Gaussian noise corruption in diffusion models with a synthetic anomaly degradation process allows a diffusion-like model to be used directly for unsupervised anomaly detection and localisation. It does this by learning a score function that generalizes to naturally-occurring medical anomalies and indicates how to modify a test image to bring it within the healthy distribution. Diffusion-like pipelines without noise have previously been proposed for image generation [14], but to our knowledge this is the first approach specifically designed for UAD.

References:

[2] Christoph Baur et al., “Autoencoders for Unsupervised Anomaly Segmentation in Brain MR Images: A Comparative Study,” Medical image analysis , , no. 02 Jan 2021, pp. 69:101952, 2021.
[3] Thomas Schlegl et al., “f-AnoGAN: Fast unsupervised anomaly detection with generative adversarial networks,” Medical image analysis , vol. 54, pp. 30–44, 2019.

[5] Xiaoran Chen et al., “Unsupervised lesion detection via image restoration with a normative prior,” Medical Image Analysis , vol. 64, pp. 101713, Aug. 2020.
[6] Sergio Naval Marimont and Giacomo Tarroni, “Anomaly detection through latent space restoration using vector quantized variational autoencoders,” in 2021 IEEE 18th International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI) , 2021.
[7] Jonathan Ho et al., “Denoising diffusion probabilistic models,” Advances in neural information processing systems , vol. 33, pp. 6840–6851, 2020.
